_readme: This file defines every gauge on the Scorecard: its data source, its polarity (which direction counts as 'better'), and its weight(s) in the composite verdict(s). Every polarity choice must be signed off by the site owner before use — see polarityJustification on each gauge. Phase E: the site now scores TWO independent dimensions (see 'dimensions' below) — Power (the original 16-gauge national-trajectory composite) and Quality of Life (new, launched with 8 gauges). A gauge's 'weights' object is the single source of truth for which dimension(s) it feeds and at what weight — a gauge with weights in both dimensions is deliberately reused (see its 'reuseNote'), never a silent duplicate. Weights are equally split within each dimension, still a placeholder pending Phase D calibration (which will now cover both dimensions together). 'accessType: api' gauges are fetched by /pipeline (run `npm run pipeline`); 'accessType: manual' gauges are entered by hand via data/manual/ — see its README.md. Until a gauge has real data, its file keeps SAMPLE_DATA status (or doesn't exist yet) and the site shows it as sample/awaiting data, never silently as live. See CLAUDE.md and METHODOLOGY.md.
_directionBasisNote: Direction (improving/flat/deteriorating) shown everywhere on the site — cards, dot strips, What's Moving — is peer-relative: it classifies the trend in Australia's level SCORE (position vs the 9-country peer set), not the trend in the raw published number. The raw-value trend is still shown, separately, in the 'Two ways to read this' block on each gauge detail page. See METHODOLOGY.md.
_staleAfterMonthsDerivation: Per-gauge staleAfterMonths derivation rule (2026-08-24 automated-gauge cadence review — see CLAUDE.md): threshold = 12 (the next reference year must fully elapse before a new data point can exist at all) + observed publication lag (months from that year's Dec 31 to when the source actually publishes it) + a small buffer. The first draft of this review dropped the leading 12 on three rows (living-standards/external-position/demographic-momentum/trade, and housing-pressure) by anchoring only to the observed lag — do not repeat that mistake at the next review. Two gauges (innovation, personal-safety) were deliberately left with NO staleAfterMonths at all: no authoritative publication cadence could be confirmed for either, and guessing one would be exactly the false precision this rule exists to avoid — they carry a staleDisclosure instead (see lib/maturity.ts's dataStaleness, which never falls back to a default for an accessType:"api" gauge left unset here).

dimensions.name: Power
dimensions.tagline: Is Australia's national trajectory rising or falling?
dimensions.description: The original 16-gauge composite: economic weight, institutional strength, and strategic position, scored peer-relative against the same 9-country set. Never combined with Quality of Life — the tension between the two verdicts is itself the point. See METHODOLOGY.md.
dimensions._scoreBandsRuling: RULED 2026-08-24 (Phase D, constitutional, not provisional): thresholds set against this dimension's own true achievable range (any of the 9 peers, any year 1990-2025: 27.1-72.2), divided into 5 equal ~9-point bands. Retired the old shared 0-24/25-44/45-59/60-79/80-100 placeholder for Power specifically. See METHODOLOGY.md's 'Phase D, Item 1' for the full options memo (three candidate schemes tested, run-length/churn decomposition, hard-constraint and proximity checks) and 'Phase D — rejected band-scheme approaches' for what was tried and rejected.

dimensions.name: Quality of Life
dimensions.tagline: Does Australia remain a good place to live?
dimensions.description: Launched Phase E (2026): a second, independently-scored composite covering health, safety, housing, work-life balance, and social cohesion. Same peer set, same min-max scoring, same maturity and provenance rules as Power — see 'Quality of Life dimension' in METHODOLOGY.md for the full gauge-by-gauge rationale and every ruling behind it.
dimensions._scoreBandsTodo: BLOCKED, not merely unreviewed (2026-08-24): recalibrating QoL's bands is on hold specifically because the historical composite series that any calibration would be run against is known-defective at its own tail — 3 of 7 QoL gauges (life-expectancy, personal-safety, air-quality) haven't reached 2024/2025 yet, so the naive AUS-anchored series forces every country's 2025 point onto a thin, non-representative 4-gauge blend (AUS: 51.4) wildly different from the real live composite (67.9, each gauge at its own latest year — a 16.5-point gap, confirmed via a hard-constraint test that every candidate scheme failed at 2025 and every candidate scheme passed at 2023, the last full-coverage year). Recalibrating on top of that would bake a data-coverage artifact into a constitutional decision. Blocked on the trajectory-series fix (Approach B: exclude thin-coverage years from computation, not just flag them in the UI — see METHODOLOGY.md and CLAUDE.md) landing and the analysis being re-run against the corrected series. Until then this dimension keeps the original shared placeholder thresholds (0-24/25-44/45-59/60-79/80-100), explicitly still provisional — Scheme 3 (42/54/68/82, centered Holding, two stable 13-14yr eras, lowest churn of any QoL candidate tested) is the standing provisional preference for the re-run, not yet ruled.

gauges.name: Living standards
gauges.polarityJustification: Higher GDP per capita, PPP-adjusted, means more real purchasing power per person — an unambiguous 'more is better' metric.

source.seriesName: GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)

gauges.oneLiner: How much real economic output there is per person, adjusted for prices.

gauges.name: Productivity
gauges.unit: GDP per hour worked (USD, constant prices, 2020 PPPs)
gauges.polarityJustification: Higher output per hour worked means the economy generates more value for the same labour input — the standard productivity definition.
gauges.dataPolicy: OECD's live SDMX endpoint for this dataflow (DF_PDB_LV) redirects to an archive endpoint carrying the annotation NonProductionDataflow=true — OECD's own metadata flagging it as not intended for automated production queries. After three fix attempts (missing Accept headers, missing references=all on the redirect, a generic unhandled server exception on the archive endpoint itself) the query never returned data. Moved to a manual lane rather than continuing to debug infrastructure OECD itself has marked non-production — see CLAUDE.md for the full history. The same numbers are downloaded by hand from data-explorer.oecd.org using the template and instructions in data/manual/, then entered into data/processed/productivity.json directly. Not fetched automatically — update it by hand periodically.

source.seriesName: GDP per hour worked (Productivity Database)

gauges.oneLiner: How much economic value an hour of work produces.
gauges._seriesIdCorrection: The brief-assumed code (PDB_LV alone, via stats.oecd.org) is dead — OECD retired OECD.Stat / the old SDMX API in favour of a new SDMX API at sdmx.oecd.org with restructured agency/dataflow/version coordinates. Verified live 2026-07-14: the dataflow still exists as OECD.SDD.TPS,DSD_PDB@DF_PDB_LV,1.0, but is itself flagged NonProductionDataflow and redirects to an archive endpoint — see dataPolicy above and CLAUDE.md.

gauges.name: Education
gauges.unit: PISA mean score (maths, reading, science average)
gauges.polarityJustification: A higher average PISA score reflects stronger measured student performance across the three tested domains.
gauges.dataPolicy: PISA publishes three separate domain scores (reading, mathematics, science), never a pre-blended figure — this gauge's value is the average of the three, computed from OECD's own published per-domain numbers, not sourced pre-averaged. Cadence was 3-yearly through 2022; OECD is moving to a 4-year cycle from PISA 2025 onward (results due 8 Sept 2026) — staleAfterMonths is set to 45 (3.75 years) to give a realistic publication-lag grace period without nagging monthly for a source that only updates every 3-4 years. Complete as of 2026-07-16: all 4 cycles back to PISA's earliest reasonable comparison point (2012, 2015, 2018, 2022) are entered, real data throughout, no fabricated back-years. 2018/2022 retrieved directly from OECD's PISA Data Explorer; 2012/2015 retrieved via NCES's (nces.ed.gov) plain-HTML republication of OECD's own published tables (a US federal statistical agency republishing OECD's numbers verbatim, not an independent or derived source) — anchor-verified against an independently-supplied value before ingest (2015 science: AUS 510, CAN 528, JPN 538, exact match) and cross-cycle plausibility-checked (no country moves more than 40 points between any adjacent cycle). Direction now computes from real cross-cycle movement (see the computeGaugeScore null-direction fix in lib/scoring.ts, 2026-07-16, which is what made a single-point gauge show 'no trend' honestly rather than a false 'flat' before any backfill existed). Earlier cycles (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009) would extend history further but weren't pursued this round.

source.seriesName: PISA mean score (maths + reading + science average)

gauges.oneLiner: How well 15-year-olds perform on a standardised international test.

gauges.name: Innovation
gauges.staleDisclosure: R&D expenditure reaches UNESCO on national survey cycles rather than a fixed annual calendar, and several countries in this peer set report on a multi-year cycle. The figures shown are the most recent each country has published — there is no newer data to fetch. This gauge therefore carries no staleness threshold; see the methodology page.
gauges.polarityJustification: Higher R&D spending as a share of GDP means more of the economy's resources are going toward developing new products, processes, and technologies.

source.seriesName: Research and development expenditure (% of GDP)

gauges.oneLiner: How much of the economy is invested in research and development.

gauges.name: External position
gauges._polarityDecision: SIGNED OFF by site owner, 2026-07-14: 'surplus = better' is a deliberate framework choice, not a claim of settled economics — see the Methodology page for the explicit caveat that this is contestable.
gauges.polarityJustification: This Scorecard treats external self-sufficiency — a stronger surplus / smaller deficit, i.e. less reliance on foreign capital — as the 'better' end of the scale. Economists legitimately debate current account polarity (a deficit can also reflect healthy foreign investment inflows); this is a stated framework choice, not an assertion that surpluses are objectively superior. See the Methodology page.

source.seriesName: Current account balance (% of GDP)

gauges.oneLiner: Whether the country is a net lender or net borrower to the rest of the world.

gauges.name: Rule of law & corruption
gauges.unit: WGI Rule of Law + Control of Corruption, averaged (estimate, -2.5 to +2.5)
gauges.polarityJustification: Higher WGI estimates mean stronger rule of law and lower perceived corruption — unambiguously better for governance quality.
gauges._seriesIdCorrection: The brief's original assumed codes (RL.EST, CC.EST) are dead on the current World Bank API — confirmed via live test call, they return 'indicator not found'. The correct current codes, verified live 2026-07-14, are GOV_WGI_RL.EST and GOV_WGI_CC.EST under World Bank source 3 (Worldwide Governance Indicators, last updated 2026-03-18). Documented per the brief's instruction to log series ID corrections here and in METHODOLOGY.md.

source.seriesName: Rule of Law & Control of Corruption, governance estimates

componentSeriesIds.name: Rule of Law - Governance estimate (approx. -2.5 to +2.5)
Control of Corruption - Governance estimate (approx. -2.5 to +2.5)

gauges.oneLiner: How strong legal institutions are and how well corruption is controlled.

gauges.name: Demographic momentum
gauges.polarityJustification: Faster working-age population growth means a larger future labour supply and growth potential — several peers in this set (Japan, South Korea, Germany) face the opposite problem of a shrinking working-age population straining growth and pensions, which this gauge is meant to surface.

source.seriesName: Population ages 15-64, total (pipeline derives year-over-year % growth from this level series)

gauges.oneLiner: How fast the working-age population is growing or shrinking.

gauges.name: Trade
gauges.unit: Share of world exports of goods & services (%)
gauges.polarityJustification: A larger share of world exports reflects greater economic weight and competitiveness in global trade — a size/influence metric, not a policy tradeoff like the external-position gauge.

source.seriesName: Exports of goods and services, share of world total (derived: country ÷ WLD aggregate)

gauges.oneLiner: How much of world trade in goods and services Australia accounts for.

bandRobustness.note: Confirmed explicitly rather than left as the implicit default: USA has no data for this gauge’s latest shared year (2025), so the bounds-exclusion test cannot move AUS’s band by construction — this is structurally guaranteed, not merely tested-and-stable like the other 17 gauges left at the (unset) robust default.

gauges.name: Economic output
gauges.polarityJustification: A larger share of world GDP (PPP) reflects greater economic weight — a size/influence metric like Trade, not a policy tradeoff.
gauges.dataPolicy: IMF's World Economic Outlook mixes its own forward projections into the published series, with no machine-readable flag in this API to tell an actual from a projection. Policy: any year from the current calendar year onward is excluded, so a forecast is never presented on this site as an achieved fact.

maturityOverride.reason: IMF blocks GitHub Actions' IP range specifically — a confirmed standing limitation (see CLAUDE.md's "Pipeline environment quirks"). The unattended monthly pipeline can never refresh this gauge; only a manually-triggered local run can. Capped at Live rather than Established, since "survived a scheduled refresh" means the automated cron, not a human re-running it by hand.

source.seriesName: GDP based on PPP, share of world (World Economic Outlook)

gauges.oneLiner: How much of the world economy Australia accounts for, adjusted for prices.

gauges.name: Debt burden
gauges.unit: Household + government debt, % of GDP (BIS Total Credit)
gauges.polarityJustification: A lower combined household and government debt burden relative to GDP means less financial fragility and less exposure to a rise in interest rates or a credit shock.

source.seriesId: WS_TC (Total Credit), borrower sectors H+G summed
source.seriesName: Credit to households & NPISHs + credit to general government, % of GDP

gauges.oneLiner: How much combined household and government debt there is relative to the size of the economy.

gauges.name: Housing pressure
gauges.polarityJustification: A lower (or slower-rising) price-to-income ratio means housing is more affordable relative to earnings — higher values mean it takes more years of income to buy a home.

source.seriesName: Analytical House Price Indicators — price-to-income ratio

gauges.oneLiner: How expensive housing is relative to income.
gauges.reuseNote: Scored in both dimensions from the same underlying data — housing affordability is both a national economic-pressure signal (Power) and a direct determinant of whether Australia is a good place to live (Quality of Life). One fetch, one data file, two independent composite contributions at each dimension's own weight. Disclosed here, on /status, and in METHODOLOGY.md's 'Quality of Life dimension' section, per the site owner's explicit condition that reuse must never be silent.

gauges.name: Human capital depth
gauges.polarityJustification: A higher share of 25-34 year-olds with tertiary education means a more highly-skilled incoming workforce.
gauges.dataPolicy: OECD's SDMX API for this series returned no matching data after three attempts with different dimension keys (see CLAUDE.md for the full debugging history). Moved to a manual lane: the same numbers are downloaded by hand from data-explorer.oecd.org using the template and instructions in data/manual/, then entered into data/processed/human-capital-depth.json directly. Not fetched automatically, so it won't refresh on the monthly pipeline run — update it by hand periodically.

source.seriesName: Educational attainment distribution — tertiary, 25-34 year-olds, % of age group

gauges.oneLiner: What share of young adults have completed tertiary education.

gauges.name: Military capability
gauges.polarityJustification: Higher military spending relative to GDP is read here as capability, deterrence, and alliance credibility, not as militarization or opportunity cost — a genuine values choice, signed off by the site owner 2026-07-14, not a factual default. Could reasonably be flipped by a future site owner, but only as a deliberate re-decision, not a silent drift — see CLAUDE.md.
gauges.dataPolicy: SIPRI's Military Expenditure Database publishes spending in several forms (current/constant USD, per-capita, share of government spending, share of GDP). This gauge uses the 'Share of GDP' figures specifically, for consistency with this project's other normalized, cross-country-comparable gauges (external-position, trade, debt-burden) — not absolute spending, which would favour larger economies regardless of actual military priority. Fetched automatically: verified live 2026-07-14 that SIPRI publishes the full database as a direct .xlsx download with no login/API key, parsed by pipeline/lib/xlsx.mjs + pipeline/lib/sipri.mjs — see CLAUDE.md.

source.seriesName: Military expenditure, share of GDP

gauges.oneLiner: How much of the economy goes toward military spending.

gauges.name: Economic complexity
gauges.polarityJustification: A higher Economic Complexity Index reflects a more diversified, sophisticated export base with more embedded knowhow — the standard reading of ECI, and uncontroversial (unlike military capability or inequality, this polarity had no real open question).
gauges.dataPolicy: Fetched automatically via Harvard Growth Lab's public, unauthenticated GraphQL API (atlas.hks.harvard.edu/api/graphql) — verified live 2026-07-14 via schema introspection, not assumed from documentation. Country IDs are UN M49 numeric codes, resolved dynamically each run rather than hardcoded (pipeline/lib/harvardAtlas.mjs) — see CLAUDE.md.

source.seriesName: Economic Complexity Index

gauges.oneLiner: How diversified and technologically sophisticated the economy's exports are.

gauges.name: Inequality
gauges.polarityJustification: A lower Gini coefficient means income is more evenly distributed across the population — the standard reading of income inequality.
gauges.dataPolicy: This gauge is scored from OECD's Income Distribution Database Gini coefficient only, signed off by the site owner 2026-07-14. The World Inequality Database's top-wealth-share figure is shown on this gauge's detail page as context (income and wealth inequality are genuinely different things) via GaugeData.contextSeries, but does not feed the composite score — keeps this gauge to one raw series like every other gauge on the site, rather than building new multi-component scoring machinery for this one case. Stays manual: OECD's SDMX endpoint for this dataflow returned a Cloudflare bot-protection page on 3/3 live attempts from this environment (2026-07-14) — rather than build a fetcher against a dataflow whose real structure was never verified, this is entered by hand via data/manual/. OECD's Gini data updates on a rolling basis with uneven lag across countries (some countries' most recent year may be 2-3 years older than others') — staleAfterMonths is set to 24 rather than the usual 15 to reflect that real, expected lag rather than treating it as always overdue. See CLAUDE.md for the full reasoning.

source.seriesName: Income Distribution Database — Gini coefficient, disposable income

gauges.oneLiner: How evenly income is distributed across the population.

gauges.name: Internal cohesion
gauges.unit: V-Dem political polarization score (interval scale, mean-centered at 0 across all country-years — not a 0-1 share)
gauges.polarityJustification: A lower score means society is less divided into hostile, antagonistic political camps — read as stronger internal cohesion. A higher score means more cross-camp hostility and discouraged interaction along ideological lines. Polarity flipped 2026-07-16 as part of the v2cacamps switch (see dataPolicy) — v2x_cspart, the prior series, was higher_is_better.
gauges.dataPolicy: Tracks V-Dem's Political polarization indicator (v2cacamps) — switched 2026-07-16 from the originally-chosen v2x_cspart (Civil Society Participation Index) after site-owner review found v2x_cspart measures civil-society consultation/participation, a different concept from the polarization/internal-order-and-disorder concept this gauge was actually specified for. v2cacamps directly matches the brief: V-Dem's own definition is 'the extent to which society is divided into hostile political camps' and political differences 'discourage interaction across ideological lines.' v2x_polyarchy and v2x_egaldem, the two alternatives weighed against v2x_cspart in the original (2026-07-14) decision, were never polarization measures either and remain correctly rejected — see CLAUDE.md for the full reversal history and why the original candidate set never included a polarization variable at all. Scale note: unlike v2x_cspart and every other V-Dem series on this site, v2cacamps is a raw, single-question expert-survey component, not one of V-Dem's smoothed 0-1 'v2x_' aggregate indices — its published values are an interval-converted score, mean-centered at 0 across all country-years (roughly -4 to +4 in practice, 0 = global average polarization), not a bounded share. A country's value can repeat unchanged across consecutive years between V-Dem's expert re-coding rounds — real data, not a gap. Automated 2026-07-16: fetched via Our World in Data's maintained, public re-publication of V-Dem, not V-Dem directly — V-Dem's own dataset download is registration-gated (no direct URL), and the only freely-fetchable file (via V-Dem Institute's own GitHub org) is a 33MB R binary (.RData) with no safe dependency-free parsing path. Every fetch's provenance.note carries OWID's own citation chain verbatim (V-Dem version -> OWID dataset -> this site) plus OWID's self-reported lastUpdated/nextUpdate for this indicator, fetched fresh each run rather than hardcoded, so a lagging republication would show up as a disclosed staleness note rather than a silently stale version string. See pipeline/lib/vdem.mjs and CLAUDE.md for the coverage verification and two OWID CSV export quirks the fetcher works around (a time-range query collapses to just its two endpoints; combining an explicit year with a country filter causes the filter to be ignored) — worked around by fetching one explicit year at a time and filtering client-side. Verified live 2026-07-16: full 1990-2025 annual coverage for all 9 peers, zero gaps, zero missing countries.

source.institution: V-Dem Institute (via Our World in Data)
source.seriesName: Political polarization

gauges.oneLiner: How divided a society has become into hostile, antagonistic political camps.

gauges.name: Life expectancy
gauges.polarityJustification: Higher life expectancy at birth directly reflects a population's health and mortality outcomes — the standard, uncontroversial reading of this World Bank indicator.
gauges.dataPolicy: Phase E launch gauge. Verified live 2026-08-06: SP.DYN.LE00.IN resolves on the World Bank API and returns real, current values for all 9 peer countries (2024 data, 78.9-84.0 years — checked via a direct API call, not assumed). Automated 2026-08-09 via the same generic World Bank route already proven across 6 Power-dimension gauges (pipeline/lib/simpleWorldBankGauge.mjs) — no gauge-specific fetcher code, just this config entry and pipeline/gauges/life-expectancy.mjs's thin wrapper.

source.seriesName: Life expectancy at birth, total (years)

gauges.oneLiner: How many years a newborn today is expected to live, on average.

bandRobustness.note: Read-only bounds-exclusion test, 2026: AUS shows Leading (80.9, 2024) with USA in the min-max bounds; Strengthening (69.6) with USA excluded from the bounds only. USA has the lowest life expectancy of the 9 peers, which currently inflates every other country’s apparent standing, including Australia’s. Score and band left exactly as computed — this is disclosure, not correction. See CLAUDE.md for the full quantification.

gauges.name: Life satisfaction
gauges.unit: Cantril ladder life evaluation, 0–10 scale (Gallup World Poll, 3-year rolling average)
gauges.polarityJustification: A higher self-reported life evaluation (0 = worst possible life, 10 = best possible life) is the standard, uncontroversial reading of the Cantril ladder question.
gauges.dataPolicy: Automated 2026-08-09. WHR's old published data panel (worldhappiness.report/data/) is dead — retired in favour of a JS-rendered dashboard at data.worldhappiness.report with no data in static HTML. Fetched instead via that dashboard's own backend API (POST /api/data with a signed x-request-token, discovered by reading the dashboard's own public JS bundle — the signing scheme is embedded in the client code, so this replicates exactly what the official frontend does, not a bypass of anything), the same route the real dashboard uses. Column meaning verified directly from the app's own source, not assumed: its embedded legend maps the 'LI' field to 'Life evaluation _ Average (3-year) _ mean' — exactly the Cantril ladder, 3-year rolling average, this gauge's spec (not 'EV', the ranking of that score, nor 'AV', a non-3-year annual variant). Full 9-peer coverage 2012-2025 confirmed live, with two genuine published gaps left as gaps: all countries in the thin 2013 edition, and GBR in 2022. This is a real, ongoing dependency on an undocumented internal API that could change without notice if WHR restructures their dashboard — see pipeline/lib/whr.mjs.

source.institution: Gallup World Poll, via World Happiness Report
source.seriesName: Life evaluation (Cantril ladder), 3-year average

gauges.oneLiner: How people rate their own lives on a 0–10 ladder from worst to best possible.

gauges.name: Personal safety
gauges.staleDisclosure: Intentional homicide counts reach UNODC only after national police and health systems reconcile their figures, and that lag varies too widely between countries to set a release calendar against. The figures shown are the most recent available — there is no newer data to fetch. This gauge therefore carries no staleness threshold; see the methodology page.
gauges.polarityJustification: A lower intentional homicide rate means fewer violent deaths per capita — the standard, uncontroversial reading of this UNODC-sourced measure.
gauges.dataPolicy: Phase E launch gauge. Verified live 2026-08-06: VC.IHR.PSRC.P5 (UNODC's intentional homicide data, hosted by the World Bank) resolves and returns real, current values for all 9 peer countries (2021-2023 data, 0.23-5.76 per 100,000 — checked via a direct API call, not assumed). Automated 2026-08-09 via the same generic World Bank route as life-expectancy and air-quality.

source.seriesName: Intentional homicides (per 100,000 people)

gauges.oneLiner: How many people are victims of intentional homicide, per 100,000 population.

bandRobustness.note: Read-only bounds-exclusion test, 2026: AUS shows Leading (88.7, 2023) with USA in the min-max bounds; Strengthening (64.3) with USA excluded from the bounds only. USA has by far the highest homicide rate of the 9 peers, which currently inflates every other country’s apparent standing, including Australia’s. Score and band left exactly as computed — this is disclosure, not correction. See CLAUDE.md for the full quantification.

gauges.name: Work-life balance
gauges.unit: Average annual hours actually worked per worker
gauges.polarityJustification: Fewer average annual hours actually worked per worker is read here as more room for life outside paid work — OECD's own commentary on this indicator uses the same reading. A genuine values choice (a reader could equally read more hours as more opportunity or income), flagged the same way military-capability's polarity is flagged in this file — not asserted as a settled fact.
gauges.dataPolicy: Moved to the manual lane 2026-08-09 after 3 automation rounds against OECD.ELS.SAE,DSD_HW@DF_AVG_ANN_HRS_WKD,1.0. Round 1: real conflict, DEU 1991, resolved by pinning WORKER_STATUS=_T ('Total') — evidence-based, not a guess (JOB_COVERAGE=_T unopposed in the same key confirmed _T is this dataflow's real Total marker). Round 2: clean save, but only 1995-2019, while a secondary source showed real OECD data through 2023. Round 3 (explicitly granted as a final round): a separate probe for 2020+ with WORKER_STATUS unpinned again surfaced a SECOND, different conflict — DEU 2023, 1299.8 vs 1338.8, WORKER_STATUS=_T vs ICSE93_1 disagreeing even in the recent window. That's structurally significant: if _T genuinely carries 2023 data, the historical query (already pinned to _T across the full range) should have returned it directly — it didn't, meaning some OTHER still-wildcarded dimension distinguishes an 'old _T' series (1995-2019) from a 'new _T' series (2020+), invisible without yet another live round. Per the site owner's explicit 'no fourth round' stopping rule, this is a genuine structural ambiguity, not a one-more-pin problem — same shape of dead end this project hit with Inequality's OECD attempt. The real 1995-2019 data already fetched is entered here as the current baseline; this gauge is now updated by hand via data-explorer.oecd.org (same source, filtered by a human eye rather than an under-constrained automated key) — see data/manual/README.md. pipeline/gauges/work-life-balance.mjs was deleted rather than left as dead code, same treatment as productivity.mjs, human-capital-depth.mjs, and inequality.mjs before it.

source.seriesName: Average annual hours actually worked per worker

gauges.oneLiner: How many hours a year the average worker actually works.

gauges.name: Air quality
gauges.unit: PM2.5 air pollution, mean annual exposure (micrograms per cubic meter)
gauges.polarityJustification: Lower mean annual PM2.5 exposure means less fine-particulate air pollution reaching the population — the standard, uncontroversial reading of this World Bank/IHME indicator.
gauges.dataPolicy: Phase E launch gauge. Verified live 2026-08-06: EN.ATM.PM25.MC.M3 resolves and returns real, current values for all 9 peer countries (2023 data, 6.4-21.9 μg/m³ — checked via a direct API call, not assumed; South Korea is a clear outlier here, worth watching once real history is loaded). Sourced from IHME's Global Burden of Disease study via the World Bank; same generic World Bank fetch route as life-expectancy and personal-safety, automated 2026-08-09. Note this indicator does not update strictly annually — GBD vintages are released periodically, not every calendar year — a missing recent year here is that publication cadence, not a broken fetch; the fetcher handles this by omission (no estimation), same as any other gauge with an uneven reporting cadence.

source.institution: World Bank (IHME Global Burden of Disease)
source.seriesName: PM2.5 air pollution, mean annual exposure (micrograms per cubic meter)

gauges.oneLiner: How much fine-particulate air pollution the average person is exposed to.

gauges.name: Cohesion — minority experience
gauges.unit: V-Dem social group equality in civil liberties score (interval scale, mean-centered at 0 across all country-years — not a 0-1 share)
gauges.polarityJustification: A higher score means social groups — defined by language, ethnicity, religion, race, region, and/or caste — are more equally free from forced labor, more equally have property rights and access to justice, and more equally enjoy freedom of movement. The standard reading of V-Dem's own definition; higher is unambiguously better here.
gauges.dataPolicy: Phase E launch gauge, the 'minority experience' half of the social cohesion cluster — paired with cohesion-majority-acceptance, with the divergence between the two surfaced as a non-scored callout on both gauge pages rather than blended into one score (site owner's explicit ruling, Step 1). Tracks V-Dem's v2clsocgrp ('Social group equality in respect for civil liberties') — a raw, single-question expert-survey component, same scale character as internal-cohesion's v2cacamps (interval-converted, mean-centered at 0, not a bounded share). Verified live 2026-08-06: Our World in Data republishes this exact indicator at ourworldindata.org/grapher/equality-of-civil-liberties-across-social-groups-score (confirmed via its metadata endpoint — description matches the v2clsocgrp codebook definition word for word) with real 2023 data for all 9 peers (range -0.33 to 3.49) — fetched via a direct CSV pull, not assumed. Automated 2026-08-09 via the same proven OWID-republication route already built for internal-cohesion (pipeline/lib/vdem.mjs, generalised into a factory the same day so both indicators share one fetch implementation), including its documented CSV export quirks (a country filter is ignored once an explicit year is present — worked around by fetching the full file and filtering client-side). Untested from GitHub Actions specifically as of this build — same caveat internal-cohesion carried at its own launch.

source.institution: V-Dem Institute (via Our World in Data)
source.seriesName: Social group equality in respect for civil liberties

gauges.oneLiner: How equally different social groups experience civil liberties — freedom of movement, property rights, access to justice.

gauges.name: Cohesion — majority acceptance
gauges.polarityJustification: A higher index score means the surveyed population is more likely to view migrants living in the country, becoming neighbours, and marrying into the family as good things — the standard, uncontroversial reading of Gallup's own index. Not actually scored — see unscoredReason — but recorded for the raw values shown.
gauges.unscoredReason: This gauge is not scored. No public source measures majority attitudes toward minorities across all nine peer countries. Gallup's Migrant Acceptance Index covered eight of the nine in 2016/17, but its 2019 update published only a global top-ten list — four of our nine, and precisely the four highest scorers (Canada, New Zealand, Australia, United States), which would bias any computed score upward rather than just leave it incomplete. Gallup continues to field the underlying question; country-level results are available only by paid subscription. The absence of a comparable public series is itself a finding.
gauges.dataPolicy: Fetched directly from the two Gallup news-release articles that publish this index's country tables — not a data product, a provenance chain disclosed explicitly on this gauge's own page. 2016/17 wave (news.gallup.com/poll/216377/...): a full ranked table, 8 of 9 peers (Canada absent — the article's own text says 'Canada will be surveyed later in 2017,' never entered this wave's table at all). 2019 wave (news.gallup.com/poll/320678/...): NOT a full table — only a global top-10 list, so only 4 of 9 peers appear (Canada, New Zealand, Australia, United States). The other 5 (UK, Germany, Japan, Netherlands, South Korea) are not published anywhere in either article — confirmed by reading both in full, not inferred. Full 5-source search record (why no better source exists) is in METHODOLOGY.md's 'Quality of Life dimension' section. Two named upgrade conditions for a later phase, recorded as the trigger for a future session to revisit, not investigated further now: (1) Ipsos Global Views on Immigration covers eight of the nine peers (~3-yearly, missing the Netherlands) — if a fuller release covering the Netherlands is found, this gauge becomes scoreable. (2) WVS Wave 8 results, expected after its December 2026 fieldwork ends.
gauges.staleDisclosure: This gauge's underlying data is genuinely 7 years old (last freely published wave: 2019) — not a slow-but-normal cadence like Education/PISA's 3-4-yearly cycle, but the practical end of what's publicly available at all. See the dataPolicy note above and 'Quality of Life dimension' in METHODOLOGY.md for the full search record behind this.
